roles: brother-in-law of the Baal Shem Tov
emigrant to the Land of Israel
summary: Abraham Gershon of Kutov (Kitov, c. 1701-c. 1761) was a talmudist and kabbalist, a member of the scholarly circle of Brody, and the brother-in-law of Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov. He is remembered chiefly as the recipient of the Besht's letter known as the 'Holy Epistle' (Iggeret ha-Kodesh), the single text most plausibly reflecting the Besht's own words, which recounts an ascent of the soul and an encounter with the messiah. Gershon emigrated to the Land of Israel in the 1740s, settling first at Hebron and later at Jerusalem, and his correspondence is a source studied by scholars of early Hasidism.
description:
Abraham Gershon of Kutov (from the town of Kitov/Kuty in the Carpathian region), who lived from about 1701 to about 1761, was a talmudist and kabbalist associated with the learned circle (the kloiz) of Brody, and the brother-in-law of Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov (his sister was the Besht's wife). In the tradition's account he was at first skeptical of his unlettered brother-in-law and only later recognized him as a hidden master; the relationship between the erudite scholar of Brody and the ba'al shem is a recurring motif in the hagiographic tales and is presented here as the tradition's attributed narrative rather than as documented event.

Gershon's lasting importance lies above all in his being the addressee of the Baal Shem Tov's best-known letter, the Iggeret ha-Kodesh or 'Holy Epistle', written to him after his emigration to the Land of Israel. In this letter, which modern scholarship treats as the text most plausibly reflecting the Besht's own words, the Besht recounts an 'ascent of the soul' undertaken on Rosh Hashanah in which he entered the palace of the messiah and asked when the messiah would come, receiving the answer that it would be when the Besht's teaching and 'wellsprings' were spread abroad. The letter has been the subject of detailed scholarly study, including of its several versions and of what it implies about the Besht's messianism (Jonathan Dauber's reappraisal of the letter; Moshe Rosman's and Immanuel Etkes's treatments of it in reconstructing the Besht), and it survives in more than one recension, a textual situation examined in that scholarship. The content and interpretation of the letter are recorded here as matters treated by the sources, and the theological claims within it (the ascent of the soul, the dialogue with the messiah) are presented as the letter's attributed narrative, not adjudicated.

Gershon himself emigrated to the Land of Israel in the 1740s, settling first at Hebron and later at Jerusalem, and letters exchanged with him are among the documents that historians use in reconstructing the world of the Besht and the early networks connecting the Hasidic circle to the Jewish communities of the Land of Israel. This entry presents Gershon on the tradition's own terms as the Besht's brother-in-law, a scholar of Brody, and the recipient of the Holy Epistle, while noting that much of the narrative about the relationship between the two men comes through hagiography and that the securely documented core is his kinship to the Besht, his standing as a talmudist and kabbalist, his emigration to the Land of Israel, and his place as the letter's addressee.

lifespan.note: c. 1701-c. 1761 CE; both years are approximate. Brother-in-law of the Baal Shem Tov (his sister was the Besht's wife) and a talmudist and kabbalist of the Brody circle; he emigrated to the Land of Israel in the 1740s (traditionally 1747), settling first at Hebron and later at Jerusalem, where he died. He was the addressee of the Besht's 'Holy Epistle' (Iggeret ha-Kodesh).

relations.note: Gershon of Kutov was the brother-in-law of Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov, and the recipient of the Besht's 'Holy Epistle' (Iggeret ha-Kodesh), the text most plausibly reflecting the Besht's own words, which recounts his ascent of the soul and dialogue with the messiah.
Gershon was a kabbalist as well as a talmudist, part of the learned circle of Brody in which kabbalistic study was pursued; given as his scholarly milieu. The kabbalah entry (a school) exists.
